los.text: Describe the presentation, investigation and management of patients with breast cancer
los.html:
EpidemiologyThe commonest cancer in UK women (about 1 in 7 lifetime risk); ~1% of cases are in men.
Risk factors
  • Age
  • Female sex
  • Oestrogen exposure (early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, late first pregnancy, HRT, postmenopausal obesity)
  • Alcohol
  • Family history / BRCA1, BRCA2 (also TP53, PALB2)
  • Previous breast cancer or DCIS
  • Chest radiotherapy (e.g. Hodgkin lymphoma)
  • Dense breasts.
Presentation
Hard, irregular, painless lump, may be fixed
Skin tethering/dimpling, peau d'orange, ulceration
New nipple inversion, bloody discharge, nipple eczema (Paget's disease)
Axillary lump
Screen-detected abnormality
Metastatic symptoms: bone pain, breathlessness, jaundice, headache
Suspected cancer referral (NICE NG12)
  • Aged ≥30 with an unexplained breast lump
  • ≥50 with nipple discharge, retraction or other concerning change in one nipple
  • Consider for skin changes suggesting cancer or an unexplained axillary lump at ≥30.
Triple assessment(one-stop clinic)
  • Clinical examination + imaging (mammography ± ultrasound if ≥40; ultrasound if <40) + core needle biopsy (histology, grade, ER/PR and HER2 status)
  • Ultrasound ± biopsy of axillary nodes.
  • Staging CT/bone scan if high risk
  • MRI for lobular cancer, dense breasts, implants, BRCA.
Pathology
  • DCIS (non-invasive)
  • Invasive ductal (no special type) ~75–80%
  • Invasive lobular ~10–15% (multifocal, bilateral)
  • ER-positive ~80%
  • HER2-positive ~15–20%
  • Triple-negative ~15% (younger, BRCA1, worse prognosis).
Management(MDT)
  • Surgery: breast-conserving surgery (wide local excision) + radiotherapy, or mastectomy ± reconstruction; axilla: sentinel lymph node biopsy if node-negative, axillary clearance or radiotherapy if positive.
  • Adjuvant: radiotherapy, endocrine therapy for ER+, HER2-targeted therapy, chemotherapy by risk, bisphosphonates (postmenopausal).
  • Metastatic: endocrine, chemotherapy, targeted therapy, palliative care.

los.text: Recall the oncological treatment of patients with breast cancer
los.html:
TreatmentDetailSide effects
ChemotherapyNeoadjuvant (shrinks tumours, especially HER2+ and triple-negative; shows response) or adjuvant; anthracyclines (epirubicin) and taxanes (docetaxel, paclitaxel)
  • Neutropenic sepsis (fever >38 °C within weeks of chemo → IV piperacillin–tazobactam within 1 hour)
  • Nausea
  • Alopecia (scalp cooling)
  • Mucositis
  • Fatigue
  • Cardiotoxicity (anthracyclines)
  • Neuropathy (taxanes)
  • Early menopause
  • Infertility (offer fertility preservation)
Radiotherapy
  • Whole breast after breast-conserving surgery (commonly 26 Gy in 5 fractions over 1 week)
  • Chest wall after mastectomy if high risk
  • Axilla if node-positive
Skin reaction, fatigue, breast shrinkage and fibrosis, lymphoedema; rarely pneumonitis, cardiac damage, second cancers
Tamoxifen (SERM)ER+ premenopausal (and some postmenopausal); 5–10 yearsHot flushes, VTE, endometrial cancer (report vaginal bleeding), cataracts
Aromatase inhibitors (letrozole, anastrozole, exemestane)ER+ postmenopausalArthralgia, osteoporosis (DEXA, bisphosphonates), hot flushes, vaginal dryness
Ovarian suppression (goserelin)High-risk premenopausalMenopausal symptoms
Trastuzumab (± pertuzumab)HER2-positiveCardiotoxicity (reduced LVEF: echo every 3 months)
CDK4/6 inhibitors (abemaciclib, palbociclib)High-risk or metastatic ER+Neutropenia, diarrhoea
PARP inhibitors (olaparib)BRCA carriersAnaemia, nausea
Immunotherapy (pembrolizumab)Triple-negativeImmune-related side effects
Bone-targeted (bisphosphonates, denosumab)Reduce bone recurrence/skeletal eventsOsteonecrosis of the jaw

los.text: Describe the role and importance of holistic care of patients with breast cancer
los.html:
• Holistic care covers the whole person through diagnosis, treatment and survivorship:
DomainExamples
PhysicalSide effects, lymphoedema, menopausal symptoms (especially on endocrine therapy), fatigue, pain, sexual function, fertility
PsychologicalAnxiety, depression, body image (mastectomy, hair loss), fear of recurrence
SocialWork, finances (Macmillan benefits advice), family and young children, caring roles
SpiritualMeaning, faith
Key peopleBreast care nurse (key worker), MDT, GP, psychology, physiotherapy (shoulder, lymphoedema), genetics referral if family history.
Tools
  • Holistic needs assessment
  • Treatment summary and survivorship (recovery) package
  • Prostheses and reconstruction
  • Support groups (Breast Cancer Now, Macmillan)
  • Exercise
  • Patient-initiated follow-up with advice on signs of recurrence.

los.text: Identify the psychosocial factors that impact on gynaecological and breast cancer patients.
los.html:
FactorExamples
Body imageMastectomy, scars, hair loss, stoma, weight change
Sexuality and intimacyVaginal dryness and stenosis after pelvic radiotherapy, dyspareunia, loss of libido, surgical or chemotherapy-induced menopause
FertilityLoss after hysterectomy, oophorectomy or chemotherapy: grief, relationship strain
EmotionalAnxiety, depression, fear of recurrence, uncertainty
Stigma and embarrassmentIntimate symptoms (delayed presentation), HPV/cervical cancer wrongly linked to sexual behaviour
Cultural and religiousModesty, preference for female clinicians, beliefs about illness
FamilyYoung children, caring roles, genetic implications for relatives (BRCA, Lynch)
PracticalWork, finances, travel to treatment
  • Support: clinical nurse specialist
    • psychology
    • psychosexual counselling
    • fertility preservation before treatment (egg or embryo freezing)
    • vaginal dilators
    • HRT where safe
    • support groups
    • Macmillan.

los.text: Describe the role of screening programmes and the evidence base for specific screening programmes (breast, cervical)
sessions: MHS: Evidence base for screening (breast, cervical)
los.html:
• Screening criteria (Wilson and Jungner): important problem
    • recognisable early stage
    • natural history understood
    • acceptable and accurate test
    • effective treatment that's better early
    • facilities available
    • agreed policy
    • cost-effective
    • continuous.
ProgrammeWho and howEvidence and harms
Breast screening
  • Women 50–70 (to 71st birthday), mammography every 3 years
  • Self-referral after 71
  • High risk (BRCA, chest radiotherapy) annual MRI from younger ages
  • Independent UK Panel (Marmot, 2012): ~20% relative reduction in breast cancer mortality
  • About 1 death prevented per ~235 women invited, but ~3 women overdiagnosed for each death prevented.
  • Harms: false positives and anxiety, overdiagnosis and overtreatment (e.g. DCIS), radiation, interval cancers
Cervical screening
  • 25–64
  • HPV primary testing: HPV-negative → recall in 5 years (Wales, and now England)
  • HPV-positive → cytology → colposcopy if abnormal (or repeat HPV in 12 months if cytology normal)
  • Prevents most cervical cancers by finding and treating CIN
  • HPV testing is more sensitive than cytology, allowing longer intervals.
  • Harms: anxiety, overtreatment of CIN (LLETZ → small risk of preterm birth)
HPV vaccinationBoys and girls aged 12–13 (single dose)Large falls in CIN and cervical cancer in vaccinated cohorts
Not screenedOvarian (UKCTOCS: no mortality benefit), endometrial
  • Inequalities: lower uptake in deprived areas
    • some ethnic minority groups
    • people with learning disabilities
    • and trans men with a cervix: aim for informed choice.

los.text: Describe the clinical presentation of breast disease in relation to pathology.
los.html:
ConditionPathologyPresentation
FibroadenomaBenign proliferation of lobular stroma and epitheliumYoung (15–35), mobile ("breast mouse"), firm, smooth, painless
Breast cystFluid-filled, distended lobules35–50, smooth, may be sudden and tender; aspirate if symptomatic
Fibrocystic changeHormonal responseCyclical lumpiness and pain before periods
Mastitis / abscessInfection (S. aureus), often lactationalPainful, red, hot, fever; continue breastfeeding, flucloxacillin; abscess → ultrasound-guided aspiration
Duct ectasiaDilated subareolar ducts, periductal inflammationPerimenopausal; thick green/cream discharge, slit-like nipple retraction
Intraductal papillomaBenign papillary growth in a ductBloody discharge from a single duct
Fat necrosisTrauma (seatbelt), surgeryFirm irregular lump that can mimic cancer: biopsy
Phyllodes tumourFibroepithelialRapidly growing large lump, 40s–50s
Gynaecomastia (men)Glandular proliferation (oestrogen:androgen imbalance)Drugs (spironolactone, digoxin, finasteride, cannabis), liver disease, hypogonadism, testicular tumour, puberty
CarcinomaMalignant epithelium invades stroma with a desmoplastic reaction
  • Hard, irregular, fixed lump
  • Invasion of Cooper's ligaments → skin tethering/dimpling
  • Dermal lymphatic blockage → peau d'orange
  • Duct involvement → nipple retraction
  • DCIS spreading into the nipple epidermis → Paget's disease (eczematous nipple)
Inflammatory breast cancerTumour emboli in dermal lymphaticsRed, swollen, warm breast with peau d'orange; mimics mastitis but doesn't respond to antibiotics

los.text: Compare the presentations of different gynaecological cancers
los.html:
CancerTypical patient / risk factorsPresentation
Endometrial (commonest gynae cancer in the UK)Postmenopausal (60s); unopposed oestrogen: obesity, nulliparity, late menopause, PCOS, tamoxifen, HRT without progestogen; diabetes; Lynch syndromePostmenopausal bleeding (early → good prognosis); intermenstrual or heavy bleeding if premenopausal
Ovarian60s; BRCA1/2, Lynch, nulliparity, many ovulations, endometriosis; protective: COCP, pregnancy, breastfeeding
  • Vague and late: persistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic/abdominal pain, urinary urgency/frequency, change in bowel habit, weight loss, fatigue
  • Ascites or mass
Cervical30s–40s; HPV 16/18, smoking, immunosuppression, not attending screening, long-term COCPOften screen-detected; post-coital bleeding, intermenstrual or postmenopausal bleeding, discharge; advanced: pelvic pain, ureteric obstruction, fistula
VulvalOlder (>70); lichen sclerosus, VIN, HPVItch, lump or ulcer, bleeding
  • Referral (NICE NG12): postmenopausal bleeding ≥55 → suspected cancer pathway (endometrial)
    • persistent ovarian symptoms (especially ≥50) → CA125, then pelvic ultrasound if ≥35 IU/mL
    • ascites or pelvic mass → urgent referral
    • cervix appearance consistent with cancer
    • vulval lump, ulceration or bleeding.

los.text: Link the pathology of gynaecological cancers to their typical presentation and histological type.
los.html:
CancerHistological typesLink to presentation
Endometrial
  • Type 1 (~80%): endometrioid adenocarcinoma, oestrogen-driven, arises from atypical hyperplasia, low grade.
  • Type 2: serous, clear cell
  • Older, not oestrogen-driven, p53, aggressive
Abnormal endometrium bleeds early → PMB → early diagnosis; test all for mismatch repair deficiency (Lynch)
Ovarian
  • Epithelial (~90%): high-grade serous (commonest; often from fallopian tube fimbriae; BRCA, p53), endometrioid and clear cell (endometriosis), mucinous.
  • Germ cell (young women): dysgerminoma (LDH), yolk sac (AFP), mature cystic teratoma (dermoid: benign; torsion), choriocarcinoma (hCG).
  • Sex cord–stromal: granulosa cell (oestrogen → PMB, inhibin), Sertoli–Leydig (androgens → virilisation), fibroma (Meigs' syndrome: ascites + pleural effusion).
  • Krukenberg (GI metastases, signet ring cells)
Transcoelomic spread over the peritoneum → ascites, omental cake, bloating: symptoms are vague so most present at stage III–IV
Cervical
  • Squamous cell carcinoma (~70–80%) at the transformation zone: HPV E6 (inactivates p53) and E7 (inactivates Rb) → CIN 1–3 → invasion
  • Adenocarcinoma (~20%, harder to detect)
Friable surface → post-coital bleeding; parametrial spread → ureteric obstruction (hydronephrosis, renal failure); bladder/rectum → fistulae
VulvalSCC (~90%): HPV-associated (younger, usual-type VIN) or HPV-independent (older, lichen sclerosus, differentiated VIN); melanomaLump or ulcer; inguinal node spread

los.text: Recall the most appropriate treatment for gynaecological cancers.
los.html:
CancerTreatment
Endometrial
  • Total hysterectomy + bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (usually laparoscopic) ± sentinel node assessment
  • Adjuvant vaginal brachytherapy or external beam radiotherapy by risk
  • Chemotherapy for advanced
  • Progestogens for fertility-sparing or frail patients
  • Immunotherapy (dostarlimab) for advanced MMR-deficient
Ovarian
  • Cytoreductive (debulking) surgery (hysterectomy, BSO, omentectomy, aim for no residual disease) + platinum chemotherapy (carboplatin + paclitaxel), neoadjuvant if extensive
  • Maintenance PARP inhibitors (olaparib, niraparib) especially BRCA/HRD
  • Bevacizumab
  • Germ cell tumours: fertility-sparing surgery + BEP.
  • Risk-reducing BSO for BRCA carriers (~35–45 years)
Cervical
  • CIN: LLETZ (large loop excision of the transformation zone)
  • Stage IA1: LLETZ/cone biopsy
  • Early (IA2–IB2): radical hysterectomy + pelvic lymphadenectomy or radical trachelectomy (fertility-sparing)
  • Locally advanced: chemoradiotherapy (cisplatin + external beam + brachytherapy)
  • Metastatic: chemotherapy + pembrolizumab
VulvalWide local excision or radical vulvectomy + groin node assessment (sentinel); radiotherapy/chemoradiotherapy
  • Late effects: lymphoedema, surgical menopause, vaginal stenosis (dilators), bladder and bowel toxicity, sexual dysfunction, infertility.

los.text: Apply the pharmacology of anti-emetic drugs and relevant evidence for their benefits to be able to choose and manage effective treatment for individual patients
los.html:
DrugTargetBest forKey adverse effects
Ondansetron5-HT₃ antagonist (gut vagal afferents, CTZ)Chemo/radiotherapy-induced (acute), post-operativeConstipation, headache, QT prolongation
MetoclopramideD₂ antagonist + 5-HT₄ agonist (prokinetic)Gastric stasis, migraine, post-opExtrapyramidal (acute dystonia, especially young women), max 5 days; avoid in bowel obstruction and Parkinson's
DomperidonePeripheral D₂ antagonistGastroparesis, nausea in Parkinson'sQT prolongation
HaloperidolD₂ antagonist at the CTZChemical/metabolic, opioid-induced, palliativeExtrapyramidal, QT
ProchlorperazinePhenothiazine D₂ antagonistVertigo, migraine, pregnancyExtrapyramidal, sedation
CyclizineH₁ antihistamine (antimuscarinic)Vestibular, motion sickness, raised ICP, bowel obstruction, post-opSedation, dry mouth, tachycardia; caution in heart failure
LevomepromazineBroad (D₂, 5-HT₂, H₁, α₁, muscarinic)Palliative second lineSedation, hypotension
DexamethasoneCorticosteroidCINV (with 5-HT₃ ± NK₁), raised ICPHyperglycaemia, insomnia, mood
AprepitantNK₁ antagonist (substance P)Highly emetogenic chemotherapy (acute and delayed)CYP3A4 interactions, fatigue
Hyoscine hydrobromideAntimuscarinicMotion sickness (patch)Dry mouth, blurred vision, confusion in older people
Pathways
  • CTZ (area postrema, outside the blood–brain barrier: D₂, 5-HT₃, NK₁: drugs, toxins, uraemia)
  • Vomiting centre (nucleus tractus solitarius: H₁, muscarinic, NK₁)
  • Vestibular (H₁, muscarinic)
  • Gut (5-HT₃ on vagal afferents from enterochromaffin cells damaged by chemotherapy; D₂/5-HT₄ motility)
  • Cortex (anxiety, anticipatory nausea: benzodiazepines).
Choosing
  • Match the drug to the cause
  • CINV by emetogenic risk: highly emetogenic → 5-HT₃ antagonist + NK₁ antagonist + dexamethasone (± olanzapine): combination improves complete response (MASCC/ESMO)
  • Pregnancy: cyclizine, prochlorperazine or promethazine first, ondansetron second line.

los.text: Identify situations or clinical signs that may indicate a person is at risk of abuse
los.html:
Situation or signConcern
Injuries inconsistent with the explanation, delayed presentation, repeated attendancesPhysical abuse
Injuries of different ages, patterned injuries (bites, belt, cigarette burns, grip marks), injuries to protected areas (inner arms, thighs, trunk, face, neck)
Partner who won't leave the patient alone or answers for them; controlling behaviourDomestic abuse, coercive control
Frequent missed appointments, non-adherence
Anxiety, depression, self-harm, substance misuse, chronic pain, unexplained gynaecological symptoms, STIs, repeated pregnancy or termination requests
Pregnancy (abuse often starts or escalates; injuries to abdomen and breasts)
Poor hygiene, malnutrition, pressure sores, untreated conditionsNeglect (older or dependent adults)
Unexplained money problems, changed wills, unpaid billsFinancial abuse
No ID documents, someone else speaks for them, poor living conditionsModern slavery, trafficking
Bruising in a non-mobile baby, inconsistent history, faltering growthChild abuse
Disability, dementia, social isolation, dependence on the abuserIncreased vulnerability

los.text: Enquire sensitively and appropriately about possible abuse during a consultation, respecting the patient’s dignity and privacy
los.html:
StepHow
See the patient alone
  • "It's our usual practice to see patients on their own for part of the consultation"
  • Use a professional interpreter, never family
Private and safe settingExplain confidentiality and its limits
Normalise"Because abuse is common, I ask everyone about it"
Ask directly"Do you feel safe at home?", "Has anyone hurt you or made you feel afraid?", "Does your partner ever control your money or who you see?"
Respond wellListen, believe, non-judgemental, thank them; don't pressure them to leave
Assess risk
  • DASH risk checklist
  • High risk (≥14 "yes" or professional judgement) → MARAC referral and IDVA (independent domestic violence adviser)
  • Children in the household → safeguarding referral
Safety plan and signpostNational Domestic Abuse Helpline / Live Fear Free (Wales); police (999 if immediate danger)
Respect autonomy
  • A competent adult can decline action
  • Share without consent only if serious risk of harm, children at risk or required by law
DocumentVerbatim quotes, body maps, photos with consent; keep notes where the abuser can't see them

los.text: Describe different types of abuse (e.g., physical, emotional, financial) and understand how abuse can escalate over time
los.html:
TypeExamples
PhysicalHitting, pushing, strangulation (a specific offence since 2022), restraint, misuse of medication
SexualRape, assault, coercion, exploitation
Emotional / psychologicalThreats, humiliation, intimidation, isolation
Coercive controlPattern of controlling behaviour: monitoring, restricting money, friends and movement (an offence under the Serious Crime Act 2015)
Financial / economicTheft, fraud, controlling money or employment
Neglect and self-neglectWithholding care, food, medication
Discriminatory, organisationalPrejudice-based; poor care in institutions
Honour-based abuse, forced marriage, FGM, modern slavery, online abuse and stalking
  • Domestic Abuse Act 2021 defines domestic abuse between people aged 16+ who are personally connected, including economic and controlling behaviour
    • children who see or hear it are victims too.
  • Escalation: abuse usually becomes more frequent and severe over time (cycle: tension → incident → reconciliation → calm).
    • High-risk markers for homicide: separation (most dangerous time), pregnancy, non-fatal strangulation, threats to kill, stalking, escalation, weapons, extreme jealousy, child contact disputes.

los.text: Perform a structured pelvic vaginal (PV) examination with confidence and fluidity, adhering to established clinical guidelines
sessions: PV and speculum with scenarios and pathology
los.html:
1Explain, consent, chaperone (record name), privacy, empty bladder; position supine with knees bent and apart (or lithotomy).
2Inspect the vulva and perineum: atrophy, lesions, discharge, prolapse (ask to cough or bear down).
3. Speculum (Cusco's)
  • Warmed, lubricated, inserted closed and sideways, rotated, opened to see the cervix (os, ectropion, polyps, lesions, contact bleeding, discharge)
  • Take swabs and a cervical sample if due
  • Withdraw slightly open, closing as you go.
4. BimanualTwo gloved fingers in the vagina, other hand on the abdomen:
Assess
Cervix: consistency, cervical motion tenderness
Uterus: size (in weeks), anteverted or retroverted, mobility, tenderness, regularity (fibroids)
Adnexa each side: masses, tenderness
Pouch of Douglas: nodules (endometriosis)
5Remove, cover, thank, discuss findings when dressed, document (including chaperone).
  • Fluency comes from practice on models: talk the patient through each step and stop if asked.

los.text: Present the findings of a normal and abnormal gynaecological examination in a structured and confident manner, ensuring clarity in communication
sessions: PV and speculum with scenarios and pathology
los.html:
Normal
  • "On inspection the vulva was normal with no lesions or discharge, and no prolapse on coughing.
  • Speculum examination showed a healthy-looking cervix with a closed os, no contact bleeding or discharge.
  • On bimanual examination the uterus was anteverted, mobile, non-tender and normal-sized.
  • There was no cervical excitation and no adnexal masses or tenderness."
Abnormal examples
FindingPresentation
Enlarged uterus"The uterus was enlarged to about 14 weeks' size, firm, irregular and mobile, consistent with fibroids"
Pelvic inflammation"Cervical excitation and right adnexal tenderness: differential PID or ectopic pregnancy: I'd do a pregnancy test and NAAT swabs"
Suspicious cervix"A friable cervix with contact bleeding: I'd refer urgently for colposcopy"
Prolapse"A cystocele visible at the introitus on straining"
Fixed uterus"A fixed retroverted uterus with uterosacral nodularity: suggestive of endometriosis"

los.text: Identify common gynaecological conditions (e.g., pelvic inflammatory disease, cervical abnormalities) that require a PV examination, speculum examination, and potentially swabs
sessions: PV and speculum with scenarios and pathology
los.html:
ConditionExamination / swab findingsManagement
PIDLower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness, discharge, feverPregnancy test; endocervical NAAT (chlamydia, gonorrhoea), HVS; empirical ceftriaxone IM + doxycycline + metronidazole (14 days); treat partners
Cervical ectropionRed area around the os (columnar epithelium); post-coital bleeding; pill, pregnancyReassure if screening normal
Cervical polyp, cervicitis, cervical cancerPolyp; inflamed cervix; friable massPolypectomy; NAAT; colposcopy
Bacterial vaginosisThin grey fishy discharge, pH >4.5, clue cellsMetronidazole
CandidaThick white discharge, itch, normal pHClotrimazole pessary or oral fluconazole
TrichomonasFrothy yellow-green discharge, "strawberry" cervixMetronidazole; treat partners
Atrophic vaginitisThin, pale, dry mucosaTopical oestrogen
Prolapse, fibroids, ovarian massesBulge; enlarged uterus; adnexal massPelvic ultrasound, referral
Missing IUD threadsNot seen on speculumPregnancy test, ultrasound, extra contraception

los.text: Take a focused and comprehensive history from a patient presenting with breast concerns, ensuring to explore relevant family and personal medical history
los.html:
AreaQuestions
Presenting complaint
  • Lump: when noticed, size change, pain, relation to the menstrual cycle
  • Pain (cyclical or not)
  • Nipple discharge (colour, bloody, single or multiple ducts, spontaneous)
  • Nipple changes (inversion, eczema)
  • Skin changes (dimpling, redness, peau d'orange)
  • Axillary lump
SystemicWeight loss, bone pain, breathlessness, headache (metastases)
Hormonal / gynaecologicalAge at menarche and menopause, LMP, parity, age at first pregnancy, breastfeeding, COCP and HRT use
Past historyPrevious breast problems, biopsies, cancer, chest radiotherapy
Family historyBreast, ovarian, prostate, pancreatic cancer; ages at diagnosis; Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry; known BRCA
Drugs and socialHRT, drugs causing gynaecomastia (men); alcohol, smoking
ScreeningLast mammogram
ICEFears about cancer
  • Family history meeting genetic referral criteria (e.g. one relative with breast cancer under 40, male breast cancer, bilateral or breast + ovarian cancer, several affected relatives) → genetics referral.

los.text: Perform a structured and systematic breast examination, assessing for abnormalities or concerns
los.html:
1Consent, chaperone, privacy; expose to the waist; sit at 45°.
2
  • Inspect with arms by the sides
  • Hands pressed on hips (contracts pectoralis)
  • and arms raised: asymmetry
  • Skin tethering or dimpling
  • Peau d'orange
  • Redness
  • Nipple inversion
  • Discharge
  • Scars.
3
  • Palpate each breast with the flat of the fingers
  • Normal side first
  • Systematically (clock face or concentric circles)
  • Including the axillary tail (of Spence) and beneath the nipple
  • Ask the patient to express any discharge herself.
4. Lymph nodesSupport the arm and palpate the axilla (apical, central, anterior, posterior, lateral groups), supraclavicular and infraclavicular nodes.
5. Describe any lump
  • Site (quadrant or clock position, distance from the nipple)
  • Size
  • Shape
  • Consistency
  • Surface
  • Edge
  • Mobility or fixation (to skin; to muscle: re-check with hands on hips)
  • Tenderness
  • Overlying skin.
6Cover, thank; if suspicious, examine for metastases (liver, spine, chest) and arrange triple assessment.

los.text: Evaluate presenting clinical information to select the most appropriate physical assessment and perform structured shoulder, elbow or wrist and hand examination.
sessions: Upper limb MSK examination. Shoulder, elbow, wrist applied clinical reasoning
los.html:
Presenting informationChoose
Shoulder pain worse on overhead activity, night pain on lying on itShoulder (impingement, cuff) ± cervical spine
Pain at the outer elbow when gripping or liftingElbow (lateral epicondylitis)
Tingling in the ring and little fingers, worse with elbow bentElbow (cubital tunnel) + hand neurology
Night-time tingling in the thumb and index fingerWrist and hand (carpal tunnel)
Fall on outstretched handWrist (scaphoid, distal radius)
  • Elbow examination:
StepDetail
LookCarrying angle (cubitus valgus/varus), swelling (olecranon bursitis), rheumatoid nodules, psoriatic plaques, tophi, scars, wasting
FeelTemperature, lateral and medial epicondyles, olecranon, radial head, ulnar nerve in the cubital tunnel
MoveFlexion (~145°), extension (0°), pronation and supination (~80° each)
Special tests
  • Lateral epicondylitis: pain on resisted wrist extension (Cozen's) or passive wrist flexion with elbow extended (Mill's)
  • Medial epicondylitis: pain on resisted wrist flexion
  • Tinel's over the cubital tunnel
  • Froment's sign
FinishShoulder and wrist (joint above and below), neurovascular
  • Shoulder and wrist/hand: see ICM Year 1 › Musculoskeletal › LOs 1, 2 and 9.

los.text: Analyse clinical findings in the context of anatomical knowledge to identify potential underlying pathologies affecting the shoulder, elbow or wrist and hand.

Numb "regimental badge" area after dislocationAxillary nerve (around surgical neck)Axillary nerve injury

Medial epicondyle pain on resisted wrist flexionCommon flexor originMedial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow)
Ring/little finger tingling, positive Tinel's at the elbowUlnar nerve in the cubital tunnelCubital tunnel syndrome
Fluctuant posterior elbow swellingOlecranon bursaBursitis (trauma, gout, infection)

Pain on Finkelstein'sAPL and EPB (first dorsal compartment)De Quervain's tenosynovitis
Snuffbox tenderness after a fallScaphoid (retrograde blood supply)Scaphoid fracture (risk of avascular necrosis)

los.text: Formulate an appropriate plan for further investigation or referral, based on clinical findings and current guidelines.
sessions: Upper limb MSK examination. Shoulder, elbow, wrist applied clinical reasoning
los.html:
InvestigationUse
X-rayFractures (scaphoid views), dislocation, OA, calcific tendinitis, erosions
UltrasoundRotator cuff tears, bursitis, tendinopathy, effusions, ganglia; guided injections
MRICuff and labral tears (MR arthrogram), occult scaphoid fracture, avascular necrosis
Nerve conduction studiesCarpal or cubital tunnel syndrome
BloodsCRP/ESR, RF, anti-CCP, urate, CK
AspirationJoint or bursa: crystals, Gram stain, culture
ReferralWhen
PhysiotherapyMost tendinopathies, impingement, frozen shoulder, epicondylitis
Steroid injectionSubacromial, carpal tunnel, trigger finger, de Quervain's
Orthopaedics / hand surgery
  • Acute traumatic cuff tear in a younger patient (early repair)
  • Recurrent dislocation
  • Scaphoid fracture (fracture clinic)
  • Severe carpal tunnel (thenar wasting, constant numbness)
  • Dupuytren's with fixed flexion (positive table-top test)
  • Failed conservative care
Rheumatology (urgent)Suspected inflammatory arthritis (persistent synovitis)
EmergencySeptic arthritis, unreduced dislocation, neurovascular compromise, red flags for malignancy (night pain, weight loss, mass)

los.text: Clearly and concisely present clinical findings from a musculoskeletal examination using appropriate medical terminology and structure.
sessions: Upper limb MSK examination. Shoulder, elbow, wrist applied clinical reasoning
los.html:
Structure
  • Side and joint examined
  • → look
  • → feel
  • → move (active then passive, in degrees)
  • → special tests
  • → neurovascular status
  • → joint above/below
  • → summary
  • → differential
  • → plan.
Example
  • "I examined Mrs X's right shoulder.
  • On inspection there was no wasting, swelling or scars.
  • She was tender over the greater tuberosity.
  • Active abduction showed a painful arc between 60 and 120 degrees, with full passive range including external rotation.
  • The empty can test reproduced pain with mild weakness and Hawkins–Kennedy was positive.
  • The arm was neurovascularly intact and the cervical spine was normal.
  • In summary, these findings are consistent with right subacromial impingement with supraspinatus tendinopathy.
  • I'd arrange physiotherapy and consider an ultrasound if weakness persists."
TerminologyAbduction, flexion, external/internal rotation, effusion, crepitus, valgus/varus, wasting, fasciculation, MRC power, ranges in degrees.

los.text: Describe the gross structure of the breast, its blood supply and changes with puberty/pregnancy/menopause.
los.html:
Position
  • on the pectoralis major fascia, from the 2nd to 6th ribs vertically and from the sternum to the midaxillary line
  • The axillary tail (of Spence) extends into the axilla (where many cancers arise: upper outer quadrant).
Structure
  • 15–20 lobes of glandular tissue, each draining by a lactiferous duct (with a sinus) to the nipple
  • Separated by fat and suspensory (Cooper's) ligaments from the skin to the deep fascia
  • Retromammary space (loose tissue) lets it move on pectoralis major.
AreolaPigmented; Montgomery's glands enlarge in pregnancy.
SupplyDetail
ArteriesInternal thoracic (perforating branches, mainly medial, ~60%), lateral thoracic and thoracoacromial (axillary artery), posterior intercostal arteries
VeinsFollow the arteries → internal thoracic, axillary, intercostal veins (→ vertebral plexus: spread of cancer to the spine)
NervesAnterior and lateral cutaneous branches of intercostal nerves T4–6; nipple = T4
StageChanges
PubertyOestrogen: duct growth and fat deposition; progesterone: lobule (alveolar) development; Tanner stages
PregnancyMassive lobulo-alveolar growth (oestrogen, progesterone, prolactin, hPL); areola darkens; secretion starts
LactationProlactin (milk production) and oxytocin (let-down)
MenopauseGlandular tissue involutes and is replaced by fat, so the breast becomes less dense (easier to read on mammograms)
  • Clinical: cancer pulling on Cooper's ligaments → skin dimpling
    • blocked lymphatics → peau d'orange
    • involvement of ducts → nipple retraction
    • tethering to pectoralis major (test by contracting it).

los.text: Describe the anatomy of the axillary lymph nodes and explain their importance in the lymphatic drainage of the breast and the skin of the trunk and upper limb and in the spread of tumours.
los.html:
• ~75% of breast lymph drains to the axillary nodes
    • the rest to the internal thoracic (parasternal) nodes (medial breast), and some to the other breast or abdomen.
Axillary groupPosition
Pectoral (anterior)Along the lateral thoracic vessels: first to receive breast lymph
Lateral (humeral)Along the axillary vein: upper limb
Subscapular (posterior)Along the subscapular vessels: back of trunk
CentralIn axillary fat: receive from the three above
ApicalAt the apex: receive from all → subclavian trunk
Surgical levelRelation to pectoralis minor
Level ILateral (below) to pectoralis minor
Level IIBehind pectoralis minor
Level IIIMedial (above) to pectoralis minor (apical)
Skin drainageAxillary nodes also drain the skin of the trunk above the umbilicus (front and back) and the whole upper limb: an enlarged axillary node can come from arm infections or melanoma, not just the breast.
Tumour spread
  • Sentinel lymph node biopsy (the first node, found with dye or radioisotope) stages the axilla
  • Positive nodes → axillary clearance or radiotherapy.
  • Clearance risks lymphoedema and injury to the long thoracic nerve (winged scapula) and thoracodorsal nerve (latissimus dorsi).
Medial tumours may spread to the internal thoracic nodes and then the mediastinum.

los.text: Recognise structures of the breast on mammography, ultrasound and MRI imaging.
los.html:
TestUsed forNormal appearanceSuspicious findings
Mammography (X-ray, CC and MLO views)Screening (NHS: women 50–71, every 3 years) and assessing lumps in women ≥40Dense (white) glandular tissue in younger women, mostly fat (dark) after menopause; pectoralis major on the MLO viewSpiculated mass, clustered microcalcifications (DCIS), architectural distortion, asymmetry
UltrasoundFirst-line for women <40 (dense breasts), and to tell cyst from solid mass; guides biopsy; axillary nodesLayers: skin, subcutaneous fat, glandular tissue, pectoralisCysts are anechoic (black) with posterior enhancement; cancers are irregular, taller than wide, with posterior shadowing
MRI (with contrast)High-risk screening (BRCA), implants, lobular cancer extent, unclear findingsGlandular enhancement varies with cycleRapid enhancement with washout
  • Triple assessment for a breast lump: clinical examination + imaging (mammogram and/or ultrasound) + biopsy (core needle).
